changedBeliefs: The 32-entry cap shared by the three SQL-keyed read-path caches was never a measured number, and it is a cliff rather than a slope. All three evict at the front and promote on hit, which is approximately LRU, and LRU is the worst possible policy for a cyclic scan: at D <= 32 distinct rotating statements every read hits, and at D = 33 the entry each read needs is the one the previous miss just evicted, so the hit rate collapses rather than degrading. Measured, the collapse is worth about half of every read — 14.0 us per read against 6.1 us — and it is FLAT from 40 rotating statements to 128, which is the signature of a cliff and would not be produced by gradual cache pressure.

Exp 266 moved the workload that reaches the cap by a factor of four without moving the cap. Under the round-robin dispatch it replaced, a sequential loop over D distinct statements was partitioned across the four reader connections — each cache saw roughly D/4, so a 128-statement application still fit inside 32 per connection. Sticky dispatch sends the whole cycle to one worker. This is the tail risk exp 266's own signal named ('a workload with well over 32 hot statements might now evict where it previously did not') and it is real, but it is a change in exposure, not a regression exp 266 introduced: at any D the per-cache miss rate past the cap was always total.

The cost of an eviction is O(capacity) in BYTES, not O(1), and that is what actually bounded the cache size. `stmt_cache_insert` reclaimed a slot by disposing `entries[0]` and compacting the array so the new entry landed at the tail, moving `(STMT_CACHE_MAX - 1) * sizeof(resqlite_cached_stmt)` on every prepare. At ~1.6 KB per entry (exp 248's measurement of the fixed-size `read_tables[64]` + `dep_columns[64]` arrays) that is 50 KB per prepare at 32 entries and 203 KB at 128. The first candidate raised the caps alone and measured a reproduced +42.1% on the never-reused-SQL lane — a regression large enough to reject the raise outright, on a workload no cache size can help.

The compaction bought no ordering guarantee, because `stmt_cache_lookup_entry` already promotes a hit by SWAPPING it with the tail rather than shifting. Entry order was therefore only approximate before the change and is only approximate after it. Reclaiming the LRU slot in place — new entry at the front, where the next eviction takes it unless something looks it up first — took the guard lane from +42.1% to a reproduced -11.9%, because the 32-entry baseline was already paying ~640 us of its 3688 us sample to shift 12.8 MB. A per-prepare cost that scaled with capacity was the reason the capacity question looked closed, and it was never the capacity's cost.

The memory price of the raise is small and it is not where intuition puts it. Peak RSS rises 0.8-1.2 MB against a ~30 MB floor for 128 entries across the writer, four readers and the reserved reader; SQLite's own `Stmt` accounting rises 70.5 -> 103.4 KiB on the release suite's 48-distinct-statement diagnostics section. What makes even that price avoidable is the entry shape: `read_tables[64]` (512 B) and `dep_columns[64]` (1 KB) are fixed-size arrays sized for a worst case, and a typical statement reads one table and a handful of columns.

The repo already had a workload past the cliff and could not see it. `benchmark/suites/sqlite_diagnostics.dart` runs 48 distinct SELECT texts in its `Statement cache footprint` section — 50% past the old cap — but it reports memory, not time, so it recorded the consequence of total statement-cache thrash as a footprint number for months without anyone reading it as a latency signal.

claims.text: Raising the three SQL-keyed read-path caps (`STMT_CACHE_MAX`, `_schemaCacheMax`, `ReaderPool.rowSizeMemoryMax`) from 32 to 128, together with in-place LRU-slot reclaim in `stmt_cache_insert`, is worth a reproduced -55.5% at 40 rotating distinct statements, -55.1% at 64 and -53.3% at 128, on a lane issuing 256 point reads per sample. Per read that is 14.0 us -> 6.1 us. The win is flat across 40-128 statements, which is the cliff signature; every lane inside the old cap (`rotate8`, `rotate24`, `rotate32`, `point1`) is neutral in two independent order-flipped collections, and peak RSS rises 0.8-1.2 MB.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · macOS 26.2 · Dart 3.12.2 · AOT CLI bundle · 4-worker pool · lane-isolated, 4 alternating-order passes, 51 samples/lane, two independent ab_drift_check pairs · host 62-72% idle · 2026-08

claims.text: The statement cache's eviction compaction cost `(STMT_CACHE_MAX - 1) * ~1.6 KB` of `memmove` per prepare and dominated the capacity question. Raising the cap alone measured a reproduced +42.1% on `churn-unique` (256 never-repeated statements per sample); removing the compaction took the same lane to a reproduced -11.9%, an improvement over the 32-entry baseline. The compaction preserved no ordering that `stmt_cache_lookup_entry`'s promote-by-swap had not already given up.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT · `churn-unique` lane in `benchmark/experiments/stmt_cache_pressure.dart`, 4 alternating-order passes per candidate version · 2026-08

claims.text: A bounded SQL-keyed cache returning the wrong entry is silent, not fatal: the caller receives a well-formed result belonging to a different statement. `test/stmt_cache_pressure_test.dart` gates this by pushing 400 distinct statements through every cache and checking each statement's identity from its result — the row it selects, the columns it projects, its parameter arity, and a stream's dependency capture after churn. Four of the five tests were verified to fail against a deliberately mismatched entry (a new `sqlite3_stmt` installed under the evicted entry's old SQL text).
claims.conditions: JIT `dart test`, 400 distinct statements against 128-entry caps · 2026-08

nextSignals: `benchmark/experiments/stmt_cache_pressure.dart` is the workload exps 071 and 073 each asked for and neither built, and it is now the durable gate for any change to a SQL-keyed cache: capacity, eviction policy, lookup cost, or entry layout. Its lane roles are worth preserving as they are — `rotate8`/`rotate24` inside the cap, `rotate32` on it, `rotate{40,64,128}` past it, and `churn-unique` where no cache can help. The last of those is the only lane in the repo that can reject a cache from getting bigger, and it did exactly that once already.

The cliff moves to 128; it does not disappear. An application with more than 128 hot statements lands in the state this run found at 33, and nothing measures where a real statement mix sits. This is the same measurement exp 264's signal named (count distinct SQL strings per second in a representative trace against the cap) and it is now worth more: it bounds a 2x cliff rather than a 40% hint.

The named follow-up is the entry, not the cap. `resqlite_cached_stmt` is ~1.6 KB almost entirely because `read_tables[64]` (512 B) and `dep_columns[64]` (1 KB) are fixed-size arrays sized for a worst case that a typical statement — one table, a handful of columns — does not approach. Sizing them from what the authorizer actually captured would shrink a common entry by roughly an order of magnitude, which would make a further capacity raise nearly free, shorten the linear scan that is the remaining `churn-unique` cost, and reduce the pool footprint exp 263 identified as where resqlite's memory actually sits. It adds a malloc per prepare, which is off the hot path by construction.

The front-insert eviction was chosen because it removes an O(capacity) cost, not because its hit rate was compared against the compacting version at equal capacity. The two are indistinguishable on every lane here — below the cap neither evicts, above it a cyclic workload defeats both — so if a future run builds a non-cyclic over-capacity workload (a hot working set plus a cold tail, say), the policy comparison is still open and the harness already has the shape to host it.

A cache-sizing change needs a negative control on its tests, and it is cheap to build. Every test here passed on the first run, which proves nothing about a cache that fails silently; installing a deliberately mismatched entry took one rebuild and showed four of the five tests catch it. Any future test whose failure mode is 'plausible data from the wrong slot' should be verified this way before it is trusted.

`benchmark/suites/sqlite_diagnostics.dart`'s `Statement cache footprint` section runs 48 distinct SELECT texts and has therefore been sitting past the old cliff for months, reporting it as a footprint number rather than a latency one. Its `Stmt` KiB reading moves 70.5 -> 103.4 with this change, which is the expected direction; it is a reporting section, not a gate, so nothing fails, but a reader comparing footprints across this merge boundary should know the cause.
